lead: Two‑way finite automata let the read head move left (L) or right (R) on the input tape. The model tests whether head motion adds power to regular language recognisers. It is useful when a designer wants to scan an input repeatedly without extra memory. Only a few syllabi include this model.
prereq: You need: deterministic finite automata (DFA) and the definition of alphabet and strings (Alphabets, strings and formal languages).

blocks.text: A two‑way deterministic finite automaton (2DFA) is a 7‑tuple M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F, ⊢, ⊣). Q is a finite set of states. Σ is the input alphabet. ⊢ and ⊣ are left and right end‑markers that are not in Σ. q₀ ∈ Q is the start state. F ⊆ Q is the set of accepting states.

blocks.where: δ(q, a) = (p, d) means: in state q reading symbol a, move to state p and move the head one cell in direction d (L = left, R = right).

blocks.text: Computation starts with the head on ⊢, in state q₀. After each move the head may read a new symbol, including the end‑markers. The input is accepted if the automaton enters a state in F and then halts (makes no further moves).
A 2DFA can simulate any ordinary DFA by never moving left. Therefore every regular language is recognised.

Conversely, any language recognised by a 2DFA is regular. The proof uses crossing‑sequences: for each boundary between two tape cells only finitely many state sequences can appear when the head crosses that boundary. This yields a finite‑state description equivalent to a DFA.

items: Fix a 2DFA M with n states.
For each tape position record the ordered list of states seen when the head moves from left to right across that position.
There are at most nⁿ different lists, a finite number.
Construct a DFA whose states are these lists. The DFA accepts exactly the strings accepted by M.

blocks.text: Hence two‑way motion does not increase the class of recognised languages. The model is studied for theoretical interest and to illustrate the limits of finite memory.
Consider Σ = {0,1}. We build a 2DFA M that accepts the single string w = 10101, a palindrome of odd length.

items: δ is defined so that the head first reads the leftmost symbol, remembers it in the state, moves right to the rightmost symbol, compares, and returns.
Start in q₀ on ⊢. Move right, read the first 1 and go to q₁ (remember ‘1’).
From q₁ move right until ⊣ is seen, passing through q₂ for each interior symbol.
When the symbol just before ⊣ (the last 1) is read, compare with the remembered 1. They match, so go to q₃ and move left.
In q₃ move left back to ⊢, ignoring interior symbols.
When ⊢ is reached, the outer pair is verified. Since the length is 5, the middle symbol 0 is automatically matched. Enter q_accept and halt.

blocks.text: The head visits the tape cells in the order: ⊢ → 1 → 0 → 1 → 0 → 1 → ⊣ → 1 → 0 → 1 → ⊢. Ten moves are performed before acceptance.

examples.question: Design a two‑way DFA that accepts the palindrome w = 10101 over Σ = {0,1}. Show the sequence of head moves, the state after each move, and the total number of moves.
steps: Step 1: Start in q₀ on ⊢. Move right, read 1, go to q₁ (remember ‘1’).
Step 2: From q₁ move right to read 0, stay in q₁.
Step 3: Move right to read 1, stay in q₁.
Step 4: Move right to read 0, stay in q₁.
Step 5: Move right to read 1, stay in q₁.
Step 6: Move right to ⊣, then move left to the last 1, compare with remembered ‘1’, match, go to q₃.
Step 7: From q₃ move left across the interior symbols back to ⊢.
Step 8: On reaching ⊢, the outer pair is verified; the middle symbol 0 needs no check. Enter q_accept.
Step 9: Halt in q_accept. Total moves = 10.
examples.answer: The automaton accepts w after 10 moves.

traps: Assuming that moving left automatically allows counting; the head has no extra memory.
Confusing the end‑markers ⊢ and ⊣ with ordinary input symbols; they are never part of Σ.
Treating the crossing‑sequence argument as a construction algorithm; it only proves existence.

quiz.q: What are the two possible head directions in a two‑way DFA?
Explain why a two‑way DFA cannot recognise a non‑regular language such as {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0}.
quiz.a: The head can only move left or right but has no unbounded memory. Any crossing‑sequence across a boundary is drawn from a finite set of states, so the language must be regular. {aⁿbⁿ} requires counting, which needs infinite memory.

quiz.q: Given the transition δ(q,1) = (p,R) and δ(p,0) = (q,L), what state and head direction result after reading the string 10 starting in q?
quiz.a: Read 1 in q → move to p, head right. Read 0 in p → move to q, head left. Final state q, direction L.

quiz.q: A student claims that a two‑way DFA can recognise the language of all strings that contain the substring 101. Identify the flaw in this claim.
quiz.a: The language { w | w contains 101 } is regular, so a one‑way DFA already recognises it. Claiming that a two‑way DFA is needed is the flaw; the two‑way capability does not add any power for this language.

quiz.q: Construct the crossing‑sequence for a 2DFA with two states that reads the string 1100. List the sequence of states each time the head crosses the boundary between the second and third cells.
quiz.a: If the automaton starts in q₀, the first crossing (rightward) may put it in q₁, then the return crossing (leftward) puts it back in q₀. A possible crossing‑sequence is [q₀, q₁, q₀].

quiz.q: Why does the presence of end‑markers ⊢ and ⊣ not increase the expressive power of a two‑way DFA?
quiz.a: End‑markers only signal tape boundaries. A one‑way DFA can treat the first and last input symbols specially, so they do not add power.

beyond: Two‑way automata appear in model checking when a system must scan a trace back and forth. They are used to study space‑bounded computation and to separate deterministic from nondeterministic log‑space. In hardware, bidirectional shift registers mimic two‑way head motion.
